title: Barramundi

names.dialect: Yalanji (or Nyungkul: the dictionary entries disagree)

names.note: Given as the Nyungkul word in the murrabal entry.

identification.basis: All three words are defined in the dictionary as 'barramundi', which on the east coast is Lates calcarifer. On Gulf rivers 'barramundi' can also mean the northern saratoga (Scleropages jardinii), so Western Yalanji usage should be checked with speakers.

summary: Barramundi (*Lates calcarifer*) has three names in the Kuku Yalanji dictionary: **judi**, **murrabal** and **kudi**, which belong to different dialects [ref:hershberger1982]. It is a big silver fish of the estuaries, mangroves and rivers, and the young fish run far up into fresh water [ref:foa-barra]. Kuku Yalanji fishermen took fish with [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera), including the many-pronged *yirrmba*, and with [plant poisons](entry:fish-poisoning), [hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines), bark [nets](entry:nets) and [earth-oven](entry:earth-oven) cooking [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1909]. Barramundi also live in the Mitchell River system on Western Yalanji country, where wet-season floods carry them up into fresh water [ref:griffith2021]. **The Gulf of Carpentaria closed season, which covers the Mitchell, runs from 7 October to 31 January** [ref:qld-closed].

sections.heading: Names
Description
sections.body:
A long, powerful fish, silver to greenish-grey or greyish-blue, with a **distinctly concave head profile**, a pointed snout, a big mouth, brown to dark grey fins and a pale belly. Its eye glows **bright red** in torchlight at night [ref:foa-barra]. Barramundi commonly reach 150 cm and can reach 200 cm. They eat mainly fish and crustaceans; the young also eat insects [ref:foa-barra].

Barramundi change sex. Most start life as males and turn into females at 3–5 years old, so small fish are almost all males and the very big fish are all females [ref:foa-barra]. That is why the law protects the biggest fish.

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body:
Barramundi live in coastal and estuarine waters, often around mangroves, in clear or muddy water. Some run far upstream and some spend their whole lives in fresh water; juveniles live in the upper reaches of rivers around undercut banks, sunken logs and overhanging plants [ref:foa-barra]. On Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, look for them in the estuaries, mangrove creeks and lower rivers from the Daintree to the Bloomfield and Annan.

**Western Yalanji country.** Barramundi are part of the Mitchell River system. Griffith University's study of the Mitchell found that barramundi which move into fresh water in the wet season grow faster than those that stay on the coast, and that big wet years produce more and bigger barramundi [ref:griffith2021]. How far up the river they reach in a given year depends on the floods and on natural barriers; the study names the Mitchell Falls as a natural barrier to fish moving upstream [ref:griffith2021]. Ask the Traditional Owners where barramundi are found near you.

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body:
Barramundi migrate from fresh water down to shallow estuarine mudflats to spawn between September and March, with peaks in November–December and February–March [ref:foa-barra]. In the Gulf of Carpentaria they spawn over spring and summer, October to March [ref:griffith2021]. The wet-season floods are when barramundi push upstream into fresh water [ref:griffith2021].

The dictionary records the dry-season fishing time: bark [nets](entry:nets) were 'dragged through the water in the dry season when the water goes down' [ref:hershberger1982]. Across North Queensland, Roth recorded that fish could be hunted at any time of year, and that the [bush fences and stone dams](entry:fish-traps) were built for the falling water after floods [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
Barramundi is a prized food fish. The Kuku Yalanji fishing kit, as recorded in the dictionary and by Roth, includes [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1909]:

- **[Spears](entry:spear-and-woomera):** *kalka* (fishing spear, and the general word for spear), *yinba* (fish spear), *yirrmba* (many-pronged fish spear) and *jindal* (spear with three prongs). Roth recorded *kalka* as the general word for spear on the Bloomfield, and gave the Bloomfield name for the many-pronged fish spear as *yirmbua* (his 1909 spelling).
- **[Nets](entry:nets):** *makarr* (fish net), woven from strips of *ngunyin* bark or from *warrur* bark.
- **[Hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines):** *badur*, as in *ngayu badurriji bundanday* 'I'm fishing (sitting with hook and line)'. Bait is *mandurr*.
- **[Fish poison](entry:fish-poisoning):** the sap of the [*miyil* tree](entry:fish-poison-plants), 'used to blind fish'.

**Food rules.** On the lower Tully River (far to the south, not Kuku Yalanji country) barramundi was one of the sea foods forbidden to young people before initiation [ref:roth1908]. The dictionary records no barramundi rule for Kuku Yalanji.

sections.heading: How it was caught and cooked
sections.body:
**[Spearing](entry:spear-and-woomera) (Bloomfield River)** [ref:roth1909]:

1. The many-pronged fish spear had (usually) **four prongs morticed into the shaft**, each with a **wooden barb**.
2. On the Bloomfield it was made of a light wood, preferably [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree). Roth was told it was first brought in from outside, but it had been made locally since before 1885.

Roth adds how such spears were used further north, around Princess Charlotte Bay: thrown **at a fish in sight**, or, in a muddy water-hole, **here and there at random** on the chance of a hit [ref:roth1909]. On the lower Tully River men **crept up on barramundi lying among the snags**, or dived, and struck them from the side or from underneath [ref:roth1901].

**Muddying the water**, which Roth found everywhere he went [ref:roth1901]:

1. Stir up a small, shallow pool with your feet.
2. Spear or club the fish as they rise to the surface.

**[Fish poison](entry:fish-poisoning) (Bloomfield River)** [ref:roth1901]:

1. Hammer bark of [*Barringtonia racemosa*](entry:fish-poison-plants) between stones until it is spongy.
2. Take it into the water and rub it there with your hands.
3. The fish are stupefied in about a quarter of an hour and can be picked up.

A second Bloomfield poison: tie fruit of *Diospyros hebecarpa* (Roth's Koko-yellanji name *ngam-boi*) into long bundles, warm each bundle over a fire, then squash it in the water [ref:roth1901]. The dictionary's *miyil* sap was smashed under water the same way, with the person wrapping it in grass to keep the sap off their skin and eyes [ref:hershberger1982].

**[Nets](entry:nets).** Roth wrote that around 1900 fish-nets were **not** used at Cape Bedford, on the Bloomfield or on the Endeavour River [ref:roth1901]. The dictionary, from later Bloomfield speakers, records *makarr* 'fish net' and bark nets 'dragged through the water in the dry season when the water goes down' [ref:hershberger1982]. Inland, Roth found that the Koko-yellanji people of the Laura used an oval-framed net they called *jikan-ikan* (his 1901 spelling). Nets of that kind, framed in [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane), were carried upright through the water by two people while friends in front drove the fish towards them [ref:roth1901].

**Killing the catch.** A common North Queensland way to kill a fish was to **bite it deeply just behind the head**, so it could not flip back into the water once thrown on the bank [ref:roth1901].

**Cooking.** Small fish are simply roasted on the coals, *dindal* 'to roast on coals' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth found shrimps, and on the Tully small fish, wrapped in wild-ginger leaves for baking [ref:roth1901]. His account of the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) (*kurrma*) at Cape Bedford and on the Bloomfield, written for meat, goes like this [ref:roth1901]:

1. Heat a number of stones well in a fire, then rake out the stones and ashes and quickly dig a hole where the fire was.
2. Line the bottom with leaves of the wild gingers.
3. Lay in the food and pack the hot stones and ashes around it.
4. Cover with more leaves or [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark), then a layer of earth and stones, and leave it to bake.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
Barramundi water is [crocodile water](entry:saltwater-crocodile). Queensland's Crocwise advice for fishing is [ref:crocwise]:

1. **Stand back** from the water's edge, never on logs or branches over the water, and keep something solid like an esky between you and the water.
2. **If your lure snags, cut the line.** Don't wade in after it.
3. **Never clean fish or throw scraps** at the water's edge or a boat ramp.
4. Take extra care at **night, dusk and dawn**.

The [plant poisons](entry:fish-poisoning) described above are poisons. *Miyil* sap can blind [ref:hershberger1982]. They are recorded here as history, not as a method to use.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**Recreational rules (Queensland).** Barramundi must be between **58 and 120 cm**, with a limit of **5 per person, or 10 per boat** with two or more people aboard [ref:qld-limits]. Closed seasons protect spawning fish. In **Gulf of Carpentaria fresh waters**, which include the Mitchell River system, the season is closed **from 7 October to 31 January**. In all other Queensland fresh waters it is closed **from 1 November to 31 January**. A few listed dams are exempt, and during a closed season you cannot target barramundi even for catch-and-release [ref:qld-closed].

**Native title.** Eastern Kuku Yalanji native title was recognised in August 2026 over about 217,884 ha, from the Annan River to the Daintree River [ref:nit2026eky], and Western Yalanji native title over 170,827 ha two days later; the Western Yalanji rights include fishing [ref:nit2026wy]. Under section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, native title holders fishing for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs do not need the licences and permits other people need [ref:nta1993]. Visitors need the Traditional Owners' permission to fish on their country.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *kuyu* 'fish'; *mala-kuyu* 'good fisherman'; *damal* 'to spear'; *mumal* 'to throw a [spear with a woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera)'; *mandurr* '[bait](entry:hooks-and-lines) (any kind)'; *wuwu-damaji* 'to go back all the time to the same place, as a good place to fish' [ref:hershberger1982].
